books.section: Topic 4.7 Expanding Democracy, A. Participatory Democracy and an Expanding Electorate

primary_sources: Daniel Webster, speech to the Massachusetts Constitutional Convention, 1820-1821

stimulus.text: Paraphrase of Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 6, Topic 4.7 A: In Massachusetts, Daniel Webster led conservative opponents of democratic reform in the Massachusetts Constitutional Convention of 1820–1821, arguing that “power naturally and necessarily follows property.” Although the Federalist Party had suffered setbacks following the War of 1812, Federalist leaders in Massachusetts were able to block several of the more egalitarian proposals of the convention. Massachusetts did eliminate property requirements for voting, but it did not eliminate the requirement that voters must be taxpayers.
stimulus.source_note: Secondary text: paraphrase of Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 6, Topic 4.7 A, with one short verbatim phrase from Daniel Webster's speech to the Massachusetts Constitutional Convention, 1820–1821. Paraphrased, not quoted, except for the phrase shown.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: Webster's claim that “power naturally and necessarily follows property” best reflects which view?

options.text: Property should be redistributed to the landless men of the state
options.misconception: Webster defended property holders, not redistribution; he wanted power to stay with them.

options.text: Voting rights should follow population, not wealth
options.misconception: That is the reformers' view; Webster ties power to property, the opposite.
Webster treats property as the safe foundation of power, not as a source of corruption.

options.text: Only property holders have a real stake in government and should vote

rationales.A: Webster defended the property holders; he never proposed sharing their land.
rationales.B: Tying votes to population is the reformers' idea, not Webster's.
rationales.C: Webster treats property as the foundation of power, not as corruption.
rationales.D: If power follows property, then men without property have no stake to protect, so in Webster's view they need no vote.
rationales.general:
1. Unpack the sentence. Webster says power follows property the way a shadow follows its object.
2. Ask who is left out. Men without property hold no power in his picture, so they need no share in choosing rulers.
3. Place him. He led conservatives who blocked the convention's more egalitarian proposals.
Background: Massachusetts did drop its property rule, but it kept the rule that voters must be taxpayers, so Webster's side still won half the fight.
Remember: “power follows property” is a claim about who counts, so ask who it leaves out.
